Great question — and honestly, the answer is one of the most elegant partnerships in all of materials science. Concrete is like a goblin that's fantastic at one thing: getting hit on the head. It can take enormous compressive loads — someone whacking it with a club — but the moment you try to *stretch* it, it cracks and fails like a goblin caught in sunlight. Steel rebar is the opposite: it's brilliant in tension, like a goblin who's amazing at being pulled by the arms but crumples when you push on him.

So in a foundation, the load path creates both stresses at once. When a footing bends slightly under load (think of it like a goblin lying across two rocks), the top gets squeezed (compression) while the bottom gets stretched (tension). Concrete handles the squeeze, steel handles the stretch, and together they form reinforced concrete — a composite that's far stronger than either material alone.

There's a bonus: they have nearly identical coefficients of thermal expansion, so they expand and contract together with temperature changes without tearing each other apart. Of course — back to the chemistry, no analogies this time.

The key player is calcium hydroxide. When cement hydrates, one of the products is Ca(OH)₂, which dissolves into the pore water solution and raises the pH to roughly 12.5–13.5. At that high pH, iron becomes thermodynamically stable as an oxide rather than a soluble ion, so a thin, dense film of iron oxides (a few nanometers thick) forms on the rebar surface. This is the passive film — it's essentially the same idea as the oxide layer on stainless steel, just iron-based.

That film is what protects the rebar: it acts as a barrier between the iron and the electrolyte (the pore water), so the anodic half-reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e−) can't proceed at any meaningful rate. Corrosion is an electrochemical process that needs both an anode and a cathode, and the passive film suppresses the anodic reaction.
